reported.title: SQL injection in full-text search query
reported.body: The search term (and owner id) are interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string rather than being bound as parameters. A caller-controlled `term` containing a single quote or SQL metacharacters (e.g. "' UNION SELECT ... --") is placed verbatim into the MATCH clause, allowing arbitrary SQL injection against the documents_fts virtual table and potentially other tables reachable from the same connection.

reported.title: Admin check in purge_user is swallowed by bare except
reported.body: purge_user wraps the _assert_admin(user) call in a try/except Exception: pass. Since Forbidden is raised as an exception, this silently discards the authorization failure and lets execution continue to delete every document and share for the target user, regardless of whether the caller is an admin. This completely defeats the 'Admins only' guarantee stated in the docstring.

reported.title: delete_document has no ownership or admin check
reported.body: delete_document deletes any document by id with no verification that the caller owns it or is an admin, unlike purge_user/stats which at least attempt an admin check. Any authenticated user can call handle_delete_document with an arbitrary doc_id belonging to another user and delete it.

reported.title: export_path does not validate filename, allowing path traversal
reported.body: export_path joins the caller-supplied filename directly onto the user's export directory without checking that the result stays inside it. A filename such as '../../../etc/cron.d/evil' (or an absolute path, which os.path.join will honor outright, discarding user_dir) lets an authenticated user write the exported JSON document to an arbitrary location on disk that the process can reach, unlike indexer.py's extract_text which does perform this check.

reported.title: write_named_report skips permission check and filename validation
reported.body: Unlike write_report (which checks permissions.has_scope and sanitizes the filename via validators.export_name), write_named_report performs neither check: it joins the raw caller-supplied filename directly onto the report directory and writes to it without any scope/permission gate. The docstring claims the filename 'arrives already checked' at the only caller, but that invariant is not enforced here, so any future or existing caller of this function bypasses both authorization and path validation, enabling path traversal writes and privilege-free report writing.

reported.title: Mutable default argument shared across calls to create_share_link
reported.body: scopes defaults to a mutable list literal `[]`. Since the function mutates it in place with scopes.append('read'), every invocation that relies on the default (i.e. every call from handle_create_share when scopes=None passes through the sharing module's own default rather than a fresh list) shares and mutates the same underlying list object across calls. Any code that later mutates the returned dict's 'scopes' list (e.g. appends another scope) will corrupt the default used by all subsequent calls that omit scopes, and the returned scopes list is not a fresh copy, so unrelated share links can end up referencing each other's scope list.

reported.title: SECRET_KEY silently falls back to a public, hardcoded value
reported.body: Config.SECRET_KEY now defaults to the literal string "dev-secret-change-me" whenever QUORUM_DEMO_SECRET is unset, instead of failing fast as before. This key is used elsewhere (auth.sign, sharing.py) to sign tokens/share links. If a production deployment forgets to set the environment variable, it will silently run with a key that is public in the source tree, letting anyone forge signatures for share links or other signed artifacts.

reported.title: list_documents no longer clamps caller-supplied limit
reported.body: The limit passed by the caller is no longer capped at Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE. A caller (any authenticated user) can now pass an arbitrarily large limit and force the query to pull an unbounded number of rows into memory, defeating the pagination protection that existed before this change.

reported.title: fetch_remote_document performs an unrestricted SSRF-prone request
reported.body: fetch_remote_document issues an HTTP GET to a URL supplied entirely by the caller, with no scheme or host allowlist. An authenticated user can point this at internal-only endpoints (e.g. cloud metadata services at 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels, or localhost services) and have the server fetch and return their contents as 'imported' document body, exfiltrating internal data or credentials.

reported.title: Share signature compared with non-constant-time operator
reported.body: resolve_share_link compares the expected and supplied signatures with `!=`, which is a variable-time comparison that leaks timing information proportional to the number of matching leading bytes. Combined with a network-reachable endpoint (share link resolution), this could allow a timing side-channel to help an attacker guess a valid signature byte-by-byte instead of brute-forcing the whole token.

reported.title: Share links never expire despite a stored TTL
reported.body: create_share_link stores an expires_in value with each share row, implying links should expire, but resolve_share_link never checks it (nor any created_at timestamp) before returning the document. As written, every share link is valid forever regardless of the TTL passed in, so a link intended to expire in a day continues granting access indefinitely.

reported.title: Admin check in purge_user is swallowed by bare except

reported.title: delete_document has no admin or ownership check
reported.body: `delete_document` deletes a document by id with no call to `_assert_admin` (or any ownership check) even though it is presented as an admin operation and is reachable via `handle_delete_document` for any authenticated user. Any logged-in user can delete any document belonging to any other user simply by guessing/enumerating doc_id.

reported.title: export_path performs no validation of filename, allowing path traversal
reported.body: `export_path` joins the caller-supplied `filename` directly onto the user's export directory with no check that the result stays inside that directory (unlike indexer.py, which validates with a commonpath check). A filename like `../../etc/cron.d/evil` or an absolute path lets an authenticated user write the exported JSON document anywhere the process has write access, resulting in arbitrary file write/overwrite.

reported.title: fetch_remote_document is an SSRF vector with no URL allowlist
reported.body: `fetch_remote_document` performs `requests.get(url, ...)` on a URL supplied directly by the authenticated user, with no scheme allowlist (e.g. blocking file://) and no host allowlist (e.g. blocking link-local/metadata addresses such as 169.254.169.254 or internal-only hosts). An authenticated user can use this endpoint to make the server issue requests to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints and read the response back through the returned document body.

reported.title: SECRET_KEY silently falls back to a known, hardcoded value
reported.body: Config.SECRET_KEY used to fail fast with `os.environ["QUORUM_DEMO_SECRET"]` when the env var was missing. It now falls back to a hardcoded string "dev-secret-change-me" via os.getenv. This key signs auth tokens and share links (see auth.sign / sharing.py). If the environment variable is not set in a real deployment, the app will start successfully with a publicly-known signing key, letting anyone forge auth tokens and share-link signatures.

reported.title: list_documents no longer clamps limit, enabling resource exhaustion
reported.body: The clamp `limit = min(int(limit), Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE)` was replaced with `limit = int(limit)`. A caller can now request an arbitrarily large page size, pulling the entire documents table into memory in one request, which is exactly the resource-exhaustion scenario the original clamp existed to prevent.

reported.title: Mutable default argument shared across create_share_link calls
reported.body: `scopes: list = []` uses a mutable default argument. When called without `scopes` (as handle_create_share does when scopes is None is not passed through... actually note handle_create_share passes None to trigger the no-scopes overload, but any other caller relying on the default), the function mutates the same list object with `scopes.append("read")` on every call. Because Python default arguments are created once at function definition time, this list keeps growing (accumulating duplicate 'read' entries) and, more importantly, is shared state across unrelated calls/users, so scopes computed for one caller can leak into another caller's share record when both use the default.

reported.title: resolve_share_link never checks share expiry despite TTL feature
reported.body: create_share_link stores an `expires_in`/`expires_at` value per share, but resolve_share_link's query and validation never check it against the current time. Every share link therefore remains valid forever regardless of the TTL passed at creation, defeating the advertised time-limited sharing feature and leaving documents accessible indefinitely via old share tokens.

reported.title: Share signature compared with non-constant-time !=
reported.body: `resolve_share_link` compares the expected and provided signatures with `!=`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. This is a timing side-channel that can, with enough samples, let an attacker recover a valid signature byte-by-byte instead of brute-forcing the whole value at once.

reported.title: reports.py imports modules that do not exist in this diff
reported.body: reports.py does `from . import audit, permissions, validators`, but none of these modules are added by this PR (and the diff shows no pre-existing files with these names). Because `app/__init__.py` now unconditionally does `from . import (... reports ...)`, importing the `app` package will raise ModuleNotFoundError and the entire package becomes unimportable, breaking every handler, not just the reports feature.
